Urinary incontinence affects more than 20% of spayed female dogs, with medium and large breeds more commonly affected. In the majority of the cases urinary incontinence is caused by dysfunction of the muscles controlling the urethral sphincter. This condition results in urinary leakage during recumbency and other activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure. Left untreated, urinary incontinence can result in urine scalding, recurrent urinary tract infections, and pet relinquishment. Current treatment can include hormone therapy and other drugs to strengthen the muscle tone of the urethral sphincter, collagen injections, or surgery. Recently, we have reported that injection of muscle progenitor cells into damaged urethral sphincters can restore normal function in dogs. Study Objective The purpose of this study is to examine the effectiveness of cultured muscle cells for the restoration of urethral sphincter function in dogs with naturally-occurring urinary incontinence. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? - Female dogs diagnosed with Urethral Sphincter Mechanism Incompetence (USMI) or "spay incontinence" and have failed standard therapy. Dogs recently diagnosed with USMI can also be enrolled in this study. - Dogs should be in generally good health and have no illnesses that may interfere with the study evaluation. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign an informed consent allowing a small muscle biopsy (approximately 0.5 cubic inches)to be obtained from your dog'sleg,under sedation and local anesthesia. The incision will be sutured and your dog will be discharged from the hospital. After the muscle cells have expanded to the required number (generally about 2 weeks), your dog will return to the hospital for injection of these cells via a surgical procedure. This will require an overnight stay so that your dog will have adequate time to recuperate while being observed. The urethral tone will be assessed through urodynamic testing at baseline and then again at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months after cell injection. This testing involves placement of a urinary catheter and measurement of the urethral pressure over the length of the urethra. The test is performed with your dog under general anesthesia. These procedures do not require an overnight stay. Client Compensation Costs associated with this study will be provided, to include study visits, anesthesia, biopsy, and stem cell injection, an estimatedworth of $2,500. gingivostomatitis (FCGS) is a poorly defined disease which causes severe and painful inflammation affecting the gums and the back of the mouth. Currently, no treatments that are available are ideal, predictable and without possible complications. In prior studies in over 20 cats, IV administration of a cats own stem cells were shown to not only be safe, but, in most cases (about 70%), substantially improved or completely resolved the stomatitis. Therefore, the purpose of this double-blinded study is to treat cats for which all current treatment modalities have failed and have a poor quality of life. Once enrolled in the study patients will return to the hospital for bloodwork at one, three, and six months. Following the bloodwork, patients will then go under anesthesia to collect tissue to process the stem cells. Approximately two weeks later patients return for stem cell administration twice, one month apart. Final recheck visits will be at three and six months after the last stem cell administration. Total enrollment time is 12 months. ELIGIBILITY:Cats diagnosed with gingivostomatitis that have had full-mouth dental extractions performed and have not responded to treatment for at least six months. Cats cannot be receiving or have received in the 14 days prior any local or systemic antibiotics or immunosuppressive medications (i.e. steroids, cyclosporine.) COMPENSATION:Owners pay for the examination fee and any necessary diagnostics needed to determine candidacy in the study. Owners are also responsible for the cost of any take home medications and complications/adverse events during the study. All other procedures are covered by the study. OWNER RESPONSIBILITIES:The initial appointment will include the examination and diagnostics to determine eligibility. If eligible, your cat will go under anesthesia and have an oral biopsy and collection of fat for the production of stem cells. After the stem cells are processed (about two weeks) your cat will return to Cornell for two treatments while under anesthesia one month apart. Epilepsy is the most common neurological condition encountered in veterinary practice. The term primary (idiopathic) epilepsy is used to describe recurrent seizures with a presumed genetic or inherited basis, for which no underlying structural or inflammatory brain disease has been identified. Most dogs with primary epilepsy are managed with antiepileptic drugs, including Phenobarbital, potassium bromide, levetiracetam and zonisamide. However, it has been estimated that up to 30% of dogs with epilepsy do not attain acceptable seizure control despite appropriatedrug therapy, and are considered refractory to treatment. The incidence of refractory epilepsy is similar in humans, with approximately 30% of patients classified as having drug resistant seizures. Furthermore, despite the recent introduction of numerous new antiepileptic medications, the overall incidence of refractory epilepsy has remained fairly consistent in humans. This appears to be the case in dogs as well. Non-medical treatment options are often explored as a means to more effectively treat patients with refractory epilepsy. Listening to Mozarts Sonata for two pianos in D major, K.448 (Mozart K.448) has been shown to have a beneficial effect on several neurological disorders in humans, including epilepsy. The hypothesis set forth in this study is that Mozart K.448 is an effective add-on therapy for dogs with primary epilepsy that are refractory to traditional AED treatments. Study Objective The primary objective of the study is to determine whether or not the playing of Mozart K.448 results in a decrease in seizure frequency in dogs with refractory epilepsy. A secondary objective is to document any adverse effects and owner-perceived changes in quality of life associated with classical music therapy. The findings from this pilot study will provide information on the potential role of music therapy in the treatment of epilepsy in dogs. Results of this study will be utilized to support the design of a larger scale, randomized controlled trial evaluating the effect of music in the treatment of refractory epilepsy in dogs. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To be eligible for this study your dog must have: - A diagnosis of primary epilepsy based on characteristic signalment and clinical features of the disease (onset of seizures between 1 and 7 years of age, a minimum 1 year history of seizures, normal neurologic exam and normal blood work and urinalysis) - A history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures with currentfrequency of >2 seizures per month - Currently being treated and at a therapeutic level with at least 2 antiepileptic medications What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To be enrolled in this study, you must provide an informed consent for participation. Day 0: Your dog will be evaluated with a full physical and neurologic examination. Blood and urine samples will be collected. If your dog fits the above criteria, they will be formally enrolled. Day 1-90: You will be asked to complete a seizure diary for at least 3 months to calculate monthly seizure frequency. If you dog has an average of >2 seizures per month during this period, your dog will remain enrolled in the study. Day 90-180: You will then be provided a copy of Mozart's Sonata K.488 (compact disc or downloaded version) with instructions on how to conduct music therapy sessions and documentation at home. For 3 months you will be required to administer a music therapy session (21 minutes)twice a day. You will be required to keep a complete daily record. Post completion of the 3 month treatment, you will be asked to return to the veterinary hospital without your dog, to return completed daily record, seizure history and complete a questionnaire on your pet's quality of life.Ashort time after the completion of your dog's treatment period (~30-40 days) you will be contacted to complete a post-study survey. The dogs will receive a physical and neurologic examination, and are eligible for enrollment if a neurologic deficit is localized to the T3-L3 spinal cord. Enrolled dogs will receive pre-anesthesia bloodwork screening, and advanced diagnostic imaging (CT and MRI) under anesthesia. Buccal swabs will be collected and tested by the University of Missouri Animal Molecular Genetics Laboratory for genetic predisposition to Degenerative Myelopathy. Owners will provide periodic updates on their dogs condition through telephone consultation and/or re-examination, and postmortem examination (necropsy) will be performed by a board-certified pathologist at the end of the dogs natural life or after euthanasia. In January 2013, a condition termed constrictive myelopathy was reported in 11 adult Pug dogs (J Am Vet Med Assoc 2013; 242:223-229). This degenerative spinal cord disease caused progressive hind limb ataxia (incoordination) and paresis (weakness) in affected dogs, often with urinary and/or fecal incontinence. Imaging studies and surgery revealed fibrous thickening of the dura mater at the thoracolumbar junction, causing spinal cord constriction. The fibrous thickening was thought to be secondary to instability of the vertebrae in the area, which was believed to be associated with hypoplasia or aplasia of caudal articular processes. Another condition reportedly common in Pugs is spinal arachnoid diverticulum (SAD), in which a fluid-filled dilation of the subarachnoid space causes spinal cord compression. The pathology of SAD may also include fibrous thickening of the dura, and since both CM and SAD appear to be common in Pugs, questions arise as to the relationship of the 2 conditions, as well as their relationships to vertebral malformations in the breed. The overall goals of this study are: 1) to determine the underlying pathogenesis (mechanisms) behind CM and SAD; 2) to assess the potential relationship of these 2 diseases; and 3) to assess the potential relationships of these conditions to previously described vertebral malformations (hypoplasia and aplasia of caudal articular processes). Dr. Patterson, a veterinary pathologist, may be contacted regarding postmortem examination of affected Pugs not officially enrolled in the study. A CD containing a MRI, along with medical records and radiology reports, must be available for such dogs. Scheduling and shipping arrangements of refrigerated (not frozen) animals must be discussed in advance, if possible. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED. Malignant gliomas are aggressive cancers of the brain that affect dogs and humans. Temozolomide (TMZ) chemotherapy and radiation are the current standard-of-care therapies for gliomas. Although TMZ has been demonstrated to slow tumor progression, gliomas tend to become resistant to it over time. One way glioma cells develop TMZ resistance is by producing a protein called connexin-43. To combat resistance, we have developed a chemotherapy drug that inhibits connexin-43 and makes glioma cells more responsive to TMZ treatment. While TMZ is a systemic drug which is taken orally, the anti-connexin-43 infusion is a sustained release formulation delivered directly to the tumor site. Thoracic duct ligation has been traditionally combined with pericardectomy by many surgeons including the authors even in dogs without any evidence of pericardial disease or constrictive pericardial physiology. Clinical signs are initially very mild and refer to a thoracolumbar spinal cord disease. Over time the clinical signs progress to lower motor neuron signs in the pelvic limbs, paraplegia, and later loss of motor function including in front legs with brainstem signs in the end stage. The mean duration of clinical course ranges from 7.7 to 20 months. Breed and also owner decision are important factors for survival since many dogs are euthanized when they reach a non-ambulatory condition. While smoking has been strongly associated with the development of lung cancer in people, no definitive risk factors have been identified for dogs. Approximately 85% of lung tumors in dogs are bronchoalveolar carcinomas, whereas the most common types of lung tumor in humans are non-small cell cancers, including squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and large cell carcinoma. The most common clinical sign reported in dogs with primary lung tumors is coughing; however, up to 30% of these tumors are found incidentally, with no apparent clinical signs. These tumors are generally visualized using chest X-rays and/or CT scan. The gold standard to obtain a definitive diagnosis is surgery to remove the lung lobe followed by histopathology. Cytological diagnosis may be attempted prior to surgery via fine needle aspirate of the lung mass, usually with ultrasound or CT guidance. Reported success rates of diagnosis using this technique range from 38% to 90% in dogs. A company we are working with has developed a novel device that aims to provide bronchoscopic access to peripheral lung tumors while providing real-time visualization of the tumor. This device could provide a novel, minimally invasive way to aspirate lung tumors in dogs, with a potentially higher possibility of obtaining a pre-surgical diagnosis. This technology could also be used in humans with peripheral lung tumors in the future. The goal of this study is to assess the ability to accurately visualize and obtain aspirates of lung tumors using a novel access/visualization and needle aspiration device in dogs with suspected primary lung tumors. At the first study visit, a blood sample will be submitted to determine your dogs blood type. Your dog will then be put under anesthesia for a CT scan of the skull and thorax. Immediately following the CT, an ultrasound-guided aspirate of the tumor will be performed to obtain a diagnosis. Once the CT images have been reviewed, we will be able to determine definitively if your dog is eligible to continue on the study. Rapamycin is an immunosuppressive that has significant anticancer activity. It has been approved for use in several human cancer indications. Anecdotal reports of Rapamycin activity in canine hemangiosarcoma and other cancer types have been made over several years, however its activity has been unpredictable. Recent genomic analysis of these cancers provides a scientific basis for this sporadic activity based on the existence of several genotypes that may each be uniquely responsive to Rapamycin. Based on its reported tolerability in dogs (alone and in combination with chemotherapy) it is reasonable to now ask if Rapamycin may improve treatment outcomes for dogs with cancer. This study will be evaluating the tolerability of a novel formulation of Rapamycin. The latest version of this study seeks to do so with a novel, oil-based formulation of the drug. The mission of Ethos Discovery is to improve health outcomes for humans and animals with complex medical problems. The goal of the Dog Aging Project is to identify the genetic and environmental factors that influence healthy aging, and to understand how these factors shape aging, through a nationwide canine study. The DAP will include the study of 10,000 companion dogs, living at home with their owners. The dogs will represent a diversity of breeds and ages, both males and females, sterilized and intact, and having a full range of health status. They will come from geographically diverse homes, and from owners of diverse ethnic backgrounds and socioeconomic status. The Longitudinal Study Population will be divided into three subcohorts, including a Foundation Cohort of 8900 dogs, a Precision Cohort of 925 dogs, and an Intervention Cohort of 350 dogs, which will partially overlap with the Precision Cohort dogs. This expansive and complex project is designed as four supportive cores and four interactive projects, each of whose functions are critical to overall success. Administration, data management, cohort recruitment and retention, and environmental data gathering will all be accomplished by the cores. Project 1, the clinical project, will analyze new measures of the phenotype of canine aging that have never before been attempted on a large scale, and will assess these novel metrics as predictors of mortality and health span. Project 2 will collect and analyze genomic data, Project 3 will collect and analyze systems biology data (metabolome, microbiome, and epigenome) to understand the mechanisms by which genome and environment exert their effects; and Project 4 is a randomized controlled clinical trial of rapamycin. The Specific Aims of Project 1 include:1) Develop and evaluate a Canine Comorbidity Index (CCI) that can be used as a predictor of mortality and clinical outcomes, and a marker of aging in the companion dog. Successful completion of this Aim will provide a practical tool that is useful for standardizing descriptions of canine comorbidity, and that elucidates the relationship between acquisition of comorbidities and risk of mortality; 2) Develop and evaluate a Canine Frailty Score (CFS) with components that are prognostic for health outcomes in the companion dog and can be used as markers of aging. Frailty in aging humans is associated with negative health outcomes. The ability to describe aging companion dogs against a standardized CFS will improve accuracy in comparisons of clinical status among dogs of varying genetic background and environment and shed light on the concept of health span versus lifespan;3) Determine whether or not age-related chronic activation of the inflammatory response (inflammaging)mediates the progression of aging in the companion dog, by developing and evaluating a Canine Inflammaging Panel (CIP). The metabolome represents a complex ensemble of small molecules that provides a biochemically defined mechanistic link between genotype and downstream phenotype. "description": "Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant tumor arising from the secretory epithelium of the walls of the bilateral anal sacs. AGASACA accounts for 17% of perianal tumors and 2% of all canine skin tumors in this species. AGASACA displays aggressive biologic behavior. It is both locally invasive and highly metastatic, with a reported metastatic rate of between 26 and 96%. Metastasis to the regional lymph nodes is frequently reported early in the course of the disease, whilst metastasis to distant sites, such as the lungs, liver, spleen and bone (and other heart, mediastinum, pancreas), is typically observed months to years later. Multiple treatment modalities have been utilized in the management of AGASACA, including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, electrochemotherapy, and various combinations thereof. Currently, there is no widely accepted 'standard of care' for canine AGASACA, other than to recommend surgical resection of the primary tumor, and to consider adjuvant therapies. Surgery alone is often inadequate in controlling either local and/or metastatic disease, although a more recent paper suggests that surgical outcomes may differ depending upon the stage of the patient, 11 and the extent of surgery performed. However, with surgery alone, local recurrence has been documented in 20 to 45% of dogs with AGASACA , and metastasis in 26 to 96% of cases. The primary purpose of this study is to evaluate the clinical impact of temozolomide in dogs diagnosed with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA). Temozolomide is a chemotherapy drug used in human oncology to treat brain tumors, malignant melanoma, and more recently several different neuroendocrine tumors. Whilst AGASACA in dogs is not embryologically of neuroendocrine origin, it does share many characteristics with those tumor types, and can also respond to similar medications. The use of temozolomide in dogs has been previously reported for brain tumors, lymphoma, and malignant melanoma. Given that there is not a standard-of-care chemotherapy protocol for AGASACA, the investigators hope that temozolomide will demonstrate significant biologic activity for this tumor type, and become part of this diseases clinical management. All enrolled dogs will ideally receive 4 cycles (1 cycle = 5 days) of temozolomide, administered by mouth, at home, on study days 0/1 through 5, days 28 through 32, days 56 through 60, and days 84 through 88 (i.e. 1 cycle every month). Hospital visits will be scheduled immediately prior to each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 0/1, 28, 56, and 84. Appropriate chemotherapy recheck visits will also be scheduled for monitoring purposes 1 week after each 5 day cycle of temozolomide, on study days 12, 39, 67, and 95. A final study recheck will be scheduled on study day 112. Blood samples,+/- urine samples, will be collected at most of these recheck visits. Re-staging imaging, including thoracic radiographs (chest x-rays) and abdominal ultrasound, will be undertaken on study days 56 and 112. There are variable recommendations around the most appropriate duration to continues antibiotics following surgery. Previous studies have shown the prolonged use of antibiotics, especially multiple antibiotics, significantly increases the potential for the development of antibiotic resistant strains of bacteria. Human studies have shown that procalcitonin (PCT) concentrations are increased in patients with sepsis and it also strongly correlates with mortality in these patients. Additionally, investigators have evaluated a PCT-guided algorithm in human medicine for the de-escalation of antibiotic use, which led to decreases in length of hospital stay and the overall duration of antibiotic therapy. The results of this work highlights PCT as a promising biomarker for monitoring the response of sepsis to antibiotic treatment. This study seeks to evaluate the PCT levels in dogs with septic peritonitis as well as in dogs undergoing abdominal surgery for non-septic reasons (intestinal obstruction) to develop a PCT-guided antibiotic treatment algorithm for dogs similar to what has been developed in humans. Another significant challenge with sepsis is its initial diagnosis. Numerous studies have shown the the rapid diagnosis and implementation of antibiotics is paramount for the treatment of sepsis. There are currently no available diagnostics with the potential to provide a confirmed diagnosis of sepsis with a short enough turn-around time to be clinically useful. The current gold standard is to submit blood samples to a laboratory for culture analysis, which typically takes 3-5 days to obtain the results. This study will be collecting blood samples from dogs with sepsis at the time of diagnosis and will then perform Next Generation Sequencing to determine the most common bacterial pathogens in the blood of dogs with sepsis. These pathogens can then be used to develop a rapid point-of-care diagnostic that could be performed within the hospital to provide a diagnosis of sepsis in a time frame that would be clinically useful. Background Canine lung tumors can occur as primary or metastatic tumors. New treatment options are needed for these types of tumors, as patient outcomes are often poor, and survival times have improved little over several decades. High Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (H-FIRE) is a novel non-thermal technique that precisely ablates tumors while sparing critical structures. H-FIRE also potentially induces an anti-tumor immune response, which may help to guard against metastatic disease development.This study proposes to evaluate the feasibility and safety of treating canine lung tumors with H-FIRE, and to evaluate the tumor immune response to H-FIRE. Because canine lung tumors are a comparative model for human lung cancer, this work may inform future studies to evaluate the use of H-FIRE in people, ultimately improving outcomes for both humans and dogs. This study is funded by the Veterinary Memorial Fund. Study Design: Dogs with suspected lung tumors will have an initial visit to determine eligibility, including relevant bloodwork, examination, and diagnostic imaging. Dogs will be transferred to the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center (ACCRC) in Roanoke, VA, where they will be monitored for 72 hours following administration of H-FIRE. Tumor resection surgery will take place at the end of the 72-hour monitoring period, and dogs will remain at the ACCRC until they are fully recovered from surgery, typically 2-3 days. Total hospitalization time for the study is approximately 5-7 days. Compensation For enrolled dogs, the study-related bloodwork, histopathological analysis of the resected tumor, and up to $1,000 of the cost of a CT scan will be paid for by the study. Oral malignant melanoma (OMM) is a highly aggressive oral tumor in dogs. The presence of spread to regional lymph nodes (LN) is a known poor prognostic indicator. Evaluation of LN status is currently performed by histopathologic examination following removal of all surgically identifiable LN in the neck region. This study aims to identify the sentinel lymph node (SLN), allowing a targeted approach to reduce the need for extensive LN resection surgery. This study will evaluate removed LNs with a new emerging diagnostic tool, optical coherence tomography (OCT), to determine if OCT imaging findings can accurately detect cancer in canine LNs. In the future, OCT may be used for intraoperative assessment of LN status to guide the extent of LN removal for individual patients.

Patients will undergo routine preoperative staging consistent with current standard of care (bloodwork, thoracic radiographs). All patients enrolled in the study will undergo sedation or general anesthesia for computed tomography (CT) of the head and regional contrast administration for sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping for surgical planning. Following CT, the SLN identified will be sampled using ultrasound guidance. External beam radiation is often used to relieve pain and control cancer, specifically primary bone cancer (osteosarcoma). It is very effective, but it can cause long-term side effects including swelling, stiffness, pain, increased fracture risk, and increased risk of secondary malignancy. Fracture risk specifically is significant yet poorly understood. We know that a subset of patients, but not all patients, are at a clinically significant increased risk of fracture following radiation therapy. We also know that if a fracture occurs, it can be very difficult to treat. In human medicine such a fracture often requires several operations and many months of recovery. In veterinary medicine, fracture following radiation therapy cannot usually be fixed, requiring an amputation or humane euthanasia. Currently the risk of fracture is assessed based on x-ray characteristics and patient symptoms. However, limited knowledge of the mechanisms or extent of changes in bone secondary to radiation treatment has decreased our ability to mitigate, prevent, or predict complications in both humans and dogs. Our goal is to explore the effects of external beam radiation in a canine model. Dogs are a large animal model for humans, in which the anatomical design, mechanics of movement, and demands of load closely reflect humans. Any discoveries will be relevant and translatable to both humans and dogs.

Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to prevent macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib therapy. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of high-dose losartan and toceranib can significantly slow tumor growth and, in some cases, stimulate significant tumor shrinkage in dogs with macroscopic OS lung metastases. More recent studies indicate that the addition of a third, experimental, and immunologically active drug called ladarixin further enhances the activity of the losartan/toceranib combination by blocking recruitment of cancer inducing cells to established microscopic metastases in the lungs. Prior clinical trials deem this 3-drug combination as well-tolerated and safe to use in dogs. The purpose of this trial is to investigate the effectiveness of losartan/toceranib/ladarixin in delaying/preventing the development of macroscopic OS lung metastases. These results will be compared to those from a recently completed trial evaluating the standard chemotherapy drug used after surgery for OS (carboplatin). If this novel combination is shown to be equivalent or superior to carboplatin therapy for delaying/preventing metastatic OS, the findings would exert a major impact on both the veterinary and pediatric osteosarcoma fields, as this 3-drug combination could be readily evaluated in future trials. Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest and affected limb. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. Following enrollment into the trial, your dog will be sent home with oral losartan and ladarixin to be given twice daily and oral toceranib to be given every other day. A biopsy of the bone tumor will also be performed prior to starting treatment providing your dog is deemed to be a good candidate for this procedure. Your dog will then return 10-14 days later for limb amputation. The tumor will be submitted for biopsy evaluation, and the diagnosis of osteosarcoma must be confirmed by this test. Toceranib will be discontinued for 3 days prior to amputation and 7 days post-amputation and will resume on Week 3. Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers in cats. It has been shown to induce remission in 60 to 100% of dogs with lymphoma. It has been administered to 4 healthy cats as a single dose with no adverse effects. The goal of this study is to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of rabacfosadine, given once every 21 days, to cats with lymphoid neoplasia. Initially your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests, which may include blood tests, urinalysis, chest X-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and fine needle aspirate of any masses. These tests are part of the routine testing done in patients with lymphoid neoplasia, and may be performed even if you decide that your pet will not participate. Your cat will then receive an injection of rabacfosadine every 3 weeks for up to 5treatments. ENROLLMENT SUSPENDED Purpose To evaluate if treatment with NPS alters immune markers and impacts treatment outcome when combined with standard chemotherapy. Background Large cell lymphoma affecting the peripheral lymph nodes (multicentric) is one of the most common cancers diagnosed in dogs, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common subtype. DLBCL in dogs is clinically and genetically similar to DLBCL in people; clinical trials in dogs are helping to identify new treatments to benefit both dogs and people diagnosed with this cancer. One of cancers strategies is to evade the immune system by suppressing immune cell recognition and the ability of these immune cells to kill cancer cells. Treatments that address this by using drugs, antibodies, or directly training a patients immune system, are becoming common in people, but we are far from curing lymphoma in dogs or people. The use of local ablative strategies to modify the immune system (AIM, or ablative immune modification) and shift it from a suppressed to an active environment has been shown to be effective in rodent models and people with other cancer types. The purposes of this study are 1.) to evaluate the impact on the number and types of immune cells and their gene expression following a single treatment to a lymph node in dogs with DLBCL, and 2.) whether NPS pre-treatment prolongs the remission time when treated with standard chemotherapy with doxorubicin. Study Design This study takes place at the Animal Cancer Care and Research Center (ACCRC) in Roanoke, VA.This is a prospective, single-blind, randomized, proof-of-principle clinical trial. Dogs will be randomized to either AIM (treatment with NPS), or placebo. Only the investigation team will know whether your dog has received AIM (NPS). Blood and lymph node needle biopsies will be obtained periodically throughout the study to monitor the immune response. All dogs will undergo standard chemotherapy treatment with doxorubicin following AIM (NPS) or placebo. Chemotherapy will be given under the direct supervision of a board-certified veterinary medical oncologist at the ACCRC. If you agree to participate in the study, we will perform the following procedures: (a) Pretreatment evaluation (screening, prior to enrollment)Before beginning treatment, your dog must undergo the following tests to determine if s/he is a good candidate to enroll in the study. 1. Complete physical exam 2. Lab work 3. Biopsy or fine needle aspirate of a lymph node read by a pathologist 4. Special testing to identify whether the lymphoma is B-cell or T-cell (immunophenotyping by flow cytometry) 5. Thoracic and abdominal imaging (b) Treatment Once your dog is enrolled in the study, there are (13) protocol clinic visits which include (1) NPS or placebo treatment under general anesthesia or heavy sedation, (5) chemotherapy treatments, (2) imaging visits, (13) blood draws, and (8) fine needle aspirates (needle biopsy) of a lymph node. Upon completion of the chemotherapy protocol, monthly exams are required to monitor for remaining in complete remission: the number of these visits will vary. Nanopulse stimulation is short bursts of electrical fields applied directly to the lymph node. It is considered painless in humans and does not generate heat. NPS treatment is expected to take 30-45 minutes. Compensation The study covers the sedation and NPS (or placebo) treatment, the collection and analysis of blood and lymph node samples for determining immune response, and $250 per chemotherapy treatment visit.The total compensation per patient enrolled is $1,430.All other costs associated with screening, the chemotherapy treatment and monitoring visits, required imaging exams at day 49, and any medications or hospital visits necessary for managing side effects are out-of-pocket. All diagnostics or procedures not covered by the study are standard, and would be performed in any pet dog undergoing evaluation and treatment for lymphoma with chemotherapy. The out-of-pocket costs may vary during the study period. As of July 1, 2021, the screening costs are estimated to be $1000-1200, the costs of imaging are estimated to be $500-700. The cost of treatments vary based on your dogs weight, and management of side effects also greatly varies. Estimates of treatment visits will be calculated specifically for your dog and provided at the time of screening.

Sinonasal caner is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed rogress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to investigate the local immune response following stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) and determine whether concurrent administration of two immune-modulating drugs, losartan and propranolol, improves positive anti-tumor immune responses in dogs with sinonasal carcinoma. Dogs enrolled into this study will be randomized to one of two groups: the first group will receive SBRT in combination with oral losartan and propranolol, and the other group will be treated with SBRT alone. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush and tumor biopsy under anesthesia. If your dog is randomized to the treatment group, he/she will receive treatment with losartan and propranolol for a minimum of 7 days prior to starting radiation therapy. All dogs will receive 3 treatments with SBRT given on consecutive days. Dogs will then return two weeks after SBRT for a physical exam and anesthesia for a nasal flush and tumor biopsy. Three, 6, 12, & 18 months after completion of SBRT, dogs will return for blood work, urinalysis, and CT scan to evaluate tumor response to treatment. A small amount of blood will also be collected for study purposes prior to treatment and at the 2-week, 3-month, and 6-month post-treatment visits. Tear production will also be tested prior to treatment and at all post-treatment visits.

Background Lymphoma is one of the most common cancers diagnosed in dogs. The current standard of care for treatment is a chemotherapy protocol that uses multiple drugs: doxorubicin, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone. This protocol, the UW-19, requires weekly clinic visits for 19 weeks, and is the most effective treatment available: >85% of dogs experience a complete clinical remission (all enlarged lymph nodes return to normal size). However, canine lymphoma is rarely cured: less than 10% of dogs are alive at two years after diagnosis. Half of dogs treated with the UW-19 will have a complete remission for longer than 8-10 months. However, the remission time is measured from the date of diagnosis to the date of cancer progression, which includes the 5 months of treatment, resulting in 3-5 months of life in remission after finishing the treatment protocol. Multiple attempts to reduce the treatment time using the same combination of drugs have failed. Our team proposes a different strategy: replacing the least effective drug in the UW-19, cyclophosphamide, with a more effective drug, temozolomide. We will reduce the total treatment time from 19 weeks to 15 weeks by giving temozolomide at the same time as doxorubicin. Temozolomide has been shown to be work well alongside doxorubicin, and to be effective in dogs whose lymphoma does not respond, or stops responding, to standard of care protocols, like the UW-19. The objective of our study is to determine the efficacy and side effect profile of THOP, a new multi-drug chemotherapy protocol, as the first-line treatment in dogs with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). This approach will reduce the treatment time by 4 weeks and the overall cost of treatment by more than $1,000. Compensation Enrollment in the study will provide the temozolomide at no charge (approximately $500-1,000), the cost of the imaging exams at week 6 (approximately $600), and $300 credit to be applied towards out-of-pocket costs. Anecdotally, improvement in pain response has been reported in children and young adults that receive chemotherapy for osteosarcoma. Similar effects have also been reported in dogs. Necrotizing Meningoencephalitis in Pug dogs (also known as Pug Dog Encephalitis, or PDE) is a devastating disease that occurs in Pugs ranging from about 6 months to 6 years of age. Common clinical signs include seizures, circling, mentation changes, and visual deficits. By the time these advanced neurological signs manifest, the inflammation/necrosis is severe in most dogs and prognosis is poor even with aggressive treatment with steroids and other immunosuppressives.In our completed exploratory study, we were able to identify systemic inflammatory changes in asymptomatic dogs with high genomic risk for the PDE. This suggests the possibility that an inflammatory process of the brain may precede the development of the widely recognized advanced clinical signs of PDE. In the proposed study, we now ask if such an early inflammatory process is associated with a clinical sign/phenotype in dogs at risk for developing PDE. If an early clinical sign/phenotype can be identified, an opportunity may exist to design future studies to initiate early therapeutic intervention with immunomodulatory therapy as a means to more effectively treat PDE. Our objective is to identify neurological exam abnormalities in Pugs with high genomic risk for developing PDE, before the onset of the advanced clinical signs normally associated with the disease. We hypothesize that such an early clinical finding will not be present in a control population of dogs without a genetic risk for PDE. For at risk pugs that have exam findings consistent with PDE, a brain MRI and CSF analysis will be performed. If abnormalities consistent with PDE are found, then immunomodulatory therapy using an allogenic stem cell preparation will be administered and the pugs will be followed over a three-year period.

The purpose of this study is to determine if the addition of a probiotic (Escherichia coli Nissle 1917(EcN)) can improve clinical outcomes when paired with a standard-of-care therapy (vinblastine/piroxicam) for canine bladder cancer - also known as urothelial carcinoma.

To determine eligibility for this study, a basic screening visit including a physical exam, blood work, chest X-rays, a fecal exam for parasites, urinalysis, and potentially a genetic test for breeds (shepherds, sheepdogs, collies, old English sheepdogs) at high risk for carrying a mutation that increases the risk of side effects with some chemotherapy drugs will be conducted. All dogs enrolled will receive standard treatment for bladder cancer including vinblastine (a chemotherapeutic delivered intravenously) and piroxicam (a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug given daily by mouth). Half the dogs enrolled in this study will be assigned to receive a probiotic (given daily by mouth) in addition to the standard-of-care therapy.

The other half of the dogs will be assigned to receive a placebo (given daily by mouth). Dogs will then undergo a standard treatment regime that includes bloodwork weekly to monitor for low white blood cell counts and IV infusions of vinblastine every 2 weeks unless contraindicated. On the first and last day of the trial, dogs will also undergo sedation/anesthesia for ultrasound and tumor measurement, cystoscopy (visualization of the inside of the bladder), biopsy (tissue collection) from the tumor, and urine collection from the bladder. Owners will be asked to provide free-catch urine and stool samples from their dog every 2 weeks and asked to complete regular questionnaires and logs of the dog's clinical signs and behavior. Owners will also be asked to provide follow-up urine and fecal samples 8 weeks after the trial conclusion.


Client Compensation:

For dogs that meet enrollment criteria and enroll in this study, screening, and subsequent medical management of your dog's bladder cancer for 8 weeks or up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy will be covered at no cost to the owner/agent. The probiotic/placebo will also be provided free of charge for the duration of the study(approximately 8 weeks or for up to 4 rounds of chemotherapy). Limited funding is also available to cover adverse events secondary to the treatment protocol and in accordance with your veterinary team's recommendations. Treatment for following the conditions will be covered as part of this clinical trial during the clinical trial period: Neutropenia, urinary tract infections (UTI) and UTI workups, vomiting/diarrhea. The owner/agent is financially responsible for all veterinary costs unrelated to bladder cancer management (e.g. food, heartworm medication, medications for other conditions). Owners are also financially responsible for all costs associated with bladder cancer management beyond the trial (e.g. after 8 weeks of treatment or 4 rounds of chemotherapy) and for diagnostics and treatments associated with presumed tumor progression. Owners are also financially responsible for adverse events or injuries unrelated to bladder cancer treatment/management.

Lymphoma is the most common malignancy in cats and small cell gastrointestinal T cell lymphoma represents a large proportion of lymphoma diagnoses in middle age to older cats. The chemotherapy drug chlorambucil is routinely prescribed to manage small cell gastrointestinal lymphoma, however, the pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) or PK of this drug in cats has not been extensively studied. Compounded formulations of chlorambucil are frequently prescribed to veterinary patients in the United States as this allows for more accurate dosing of the medication to our smaller patients. However, we have previously demonstrated that the potency of compounded formulations of oral chemotherapy medications may differ by more than 10% of the labelled strength. This discrepancy in dosing could lead to under- or over-dosing of patients. To understand the potential clinical impact that use of compounded formulations may have in cats with lymphoma, a foundational understanding of the PK properties and relative bioavailability (how much active drug is absorbed by the body) of compounded chlorambucil is essential.In this study, we seek to better understand the PK, relative bioavailability, and potency of compounded formulations of chlorambucil in cats with small cell GI lymphoma. The night before their visit, cats will need to be fasted starting at midnight but can have access to water. This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) assesses the safety and effectiveness of ch45H1, a novel anticancer agent, when given to dogs with cancer. This medication is designed to help your dog’s immune system fight their cancer. The data from this study will be used to assist in the development of additional novel cancer agents in humans.

ch45H1 will be given by intravenous (IV, injection into the vein) infusion to your dog on Days 1, 22, 43, and 64 (once every 3 weeks) for a total of 4 doses. This drug is given over 90 minutes following pre-treatment with an anti-nausea medication (ondansetron), a histamine blocker (diphenhydramine), and intravenous fluids.

Within this study, we ask that you permit serial biopsies of your dog’s tumor. A biopsy will be collected prior to the first dose of drug (pre-treatment), on Day 29 and possibly on Day 85, depending on how your dog has responded to therapy. Each of these biopsy sessions will occur under anesthesia, either local (sedation with anesthetic) or general. Your dog will return to the Veterinary Teaching Hospital on Days 21 and 22, 29, 42 and 43, 63 and 64, and 85. Serial blood collections will occur on Days 1, 21-22, 42-43, and 63-64 of the study. Single time point collections will occur on Day 29. Chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound will be performed for staging purposes prior to treatment and at Days 42 and 85.

If your dog’s cancer responds well to the treatment they receive, you will be asked to participate in an additional follow-up period of up to one (1) years’ time. During that time, you will need to continue to regularly (every 8 weeks) visit the Veterinary Teaching Hospital for examination, tumor evaluation (chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, and blood collection. At the conclusion of the study, your dog will undergo a final tumor biopsy.

Cancer cells have a unique metabolism that is highly dependent on the abundance of glucose. Recent studies in mice have shown that calorie restriction slows cancer progression and improves response to chemotherapy. Other studies in dogs and people have also shown that short-term fasting can reduce chemotherapy side effects. It is not clear yet why this happens, but it is suspected that fasting positively impacts a patient's immune system and how it responds to their cancer. The purpose of this study is to learn more about how the tissue environment and immune responses that surround a tumor might be changed by short-term (48-hour) fasting.


Dogs will be screened at the screening visit (day -14 to day -1) and eligible dogs will be randomized and enrolled on Day 0 at which point a continuous glucose monitor and baseline clinical data will be collected; fasting, if applicable, will begin. All dogs will remain in the hospital starting on day 0 through Day 2 during which blood, urine, feces, and rectal and oral swabs will be collected. Day 2 (48 hours post fasting) will mark the completion of study participation and then care will be transferred to the surgical team for surgical excision per standard of care and discharge to owners. 

 

The duration of the study is 48 hours.

For dogs that meet all the criteria to participate, the cost of the initial biopsy, the hospitalization for the fasting period and all the related lab work and sample collection for the two-day study will be paid for by the study. These dogs and their owners will also receive $500 to use toward their dog's cancer treatment at the OSU Veterinary Medical Center.

Mast cell tumor (MCT) is the most common malignant cutaneous tumor in dogs. While surgery remains the mainstay of treatment for most MCT, a subset has a high potential for eventual recurrence and metastasis and require systemic medical therapy following surgery in an attempt to delay or prevent eventual metastasis. Furthermore, some dogs may present with disease that is not amenable to resection owing to size, location, or multifocal or disseminated disease. Medical therapy for these patients remains suboptimal. Gilvetmab is a drug that works by targeting key regulators of the immune system and is conditionally approved for use in dogs. Toceranib phosphate (TOC, PalladiaTM) is a targeted therapy that is approved for use in dogs with MCT. Both gilvetmab and TOC have some reported activity against MCT in the gross disease setting; however, the combination has not been evaluated for safety or efficacy in any tumor type.

The primary objective of this study is to characterize the antitumor effects and adverse effect profile of combined treatment with gilvetmab and toceranib in dogs with measurable MCT.

All dogs will be treated with TOC (oral medication given every other day) and gilvetmab (given as an IV infusion every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. They will also have concurrent treatment with certirizine and omeprazole. Visits will be required every 2 weeks until the week 20 visit. CBC only will be performed for the first 2 visits, and CBC, chemistry profile, UA/UPC, BP +/- imaging will be done every 6 weeks. If dogs have a complete response at the week 20 visit (i.e. tumor is no longer present), they will stop all treatment and come for monitoring visits every 6 weeks. Dogs whose tumors are still present will continue on TOC and recheck every 6 weeks for diagnostics. If at any point your dog’s disease progresses or they experience unacceptable side effects from the study medications, they will be withdrawn from the clinical trial.

Total hip replacement is performed in dogs affected by severe hip joint disease. Extradural anesthesia is the administration of a drug (i.e. bupivacaine) in the proximity of the spinal cord that causes a temporary loss of sensation of the dog’s back limbs. The use of extradural anesthesia in dogs undergoing total hip replacement can reduce pain and the amount of general anesthetic needed during surgery.

Major complications requiring a second surgery have been reported in about 10% of dogs after total hip replacement. It has been speculated that complications might be more likely if extradural anesthesia with bupivacaine is used. However, a recent study performed in the United Kingdom found that only 5.8% of dogs needed revision surgery after total hip replacement, despite extradural anesthesia being performed. Furthermore, none of these complications occurred during the first 24 hours post-surgery, reducing the likelihood that extradural anesthesia played a role in their development. To confirm those results, we would like to perform this study to prove that extradural anesthesia will not affect the post-surgical complication rate and the need for revision surgery, but will decrease the overall pain and analgesic consumption, improve the postoperative food intake, facilitating the recovery process of your dog.

Urethral obstruction (UO) is a common presentation for cats to the ER. Approximately 12% of those cats may have severe hyperkalemia. [Lee] Not only is this a life-threatening electrolyte derangement but it can add considerable cost to care due to prolonged hospitalization, monitoring, injectable medications and repeated blood work. Injectable calcium will stabilize the cardiac rhythm temporarily but does not alter the blood level of potassium ([K]). Ultimately, restoration of urine flow and IV fluid therapy will allow [K] loss, but may be unpredictable and for some cats with acute kidney injury (AKI), it may not be enough in the short term to guard against arrhythmias. In a recent study, UO cats with severe hyperkalemia had a lower survival rate to discharge (80%) than that reported for feline UO overall (89-95%). [Jones]

Relief of obstruction and administration of a balanced isotonic fluid therapy is the current gold-standard treatment for feline UO. [Cosford, Drobatz] There are a number of ancillary treatment options for hyperkalemia in the ER, including co-administration of insulin and dextrose (I/D), dextrose alone, bicarbonate, and albuterol. [Jones, Kline, Lindner] The efficacy of any of these treatments vs. simply restoring urine flow has not been adequately studied, but there is evidence that these ancillary treatments can increase complications. [Jones, Lindner] All ancillary treatments will increase the transport of [K] into the intracellular compartment but may not directly cause [K] loss. [Kline, Lindner] Given the rising cost of care for these patients and an increased risk of complications with insulin and bicarbonate [Jones], it is important to establish treatment efficacy when possible. While there are some comparative studies in feline UO regarding treatment protocols [Canei, Cunha, Finco, Freitas, Drobatz], there are no studies directly comparing the use of ancillary treatments vs. IV fluids alone in the treatment of severe hyperkalemia.

Our study, TSK-UO, is both a practical and academic endeavor in the ECC field. The practical goal of this study is to provide reliable treatment guidelines for ER veterinarians and move away from unnecessary treatments that have become “dogma by extrapolation.” By reducing the cost of lab work and hospitalization, we could decrease unnecessary complications and euthanasia. Secondarily, we would monitor potassium handling by the kidney post relief of the obstruction in order to investigate the mechanism and kinetics of potassium loss between treatment groups to complete a pathophysiologic map.

This study will enroll dogs with chronic diarrhea into one of two groups. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.

Uremic toxins are substances that build up in the body due to decreased removal by the kidney. They are increased in patients with CKD and correlated to severity of disease. Indoxyl sulfate is one of the most studied uremic toxins and comes from byproducts of protein metabolism in the gut. It is thought to contribute to progression of CKD including increasing fibrosis and inflammation in the kidney as well as affecting other body systems such as the heart, bones, and muscle. Porus One (Renaltec) is a new patented pure carbon product that acts as an absorbent of the protein byproduct so that it cannot be absorbed and converted into indoxyl sulfate. Instead, it is excreted in the feces. Porus One has been shown to decrease indoxyl sulfate in normal geriatric cats. The purpose of this study is to assess its effect in cats with CKD.


At the time of screening, a complete history of diet and medications will be discussed. Your cat will receive a physical examination and comprehensive laboratory screening to confirm stage of CKD and exclude other newly diagnosed conditions (e.g. hyperthyroidism, hypertension). This will also be the first time you fill out a quality-of-life survey and provide a fecal sample you have collected from your cat. Your cat will need to be in the same fed state for every visit (either fasted or fed).

After confirmation of enrollment, your cat will be randomized to start in one of the groups. This is a 16-week crossover study, meaning each cat will be in either the Porus One + standard of care group, or standard of care only group for 8 weeks and then cross over to the opposite group. Porus One will be administered sprinkled into wet food or cat snacks (e.g. Churu) once a day for a total of 8 weeks. Administration should be greater than two hours from the time other medications are given.

The study team will check in with you every two weeks by email or phone to address any questions or concerns. No changes in medication or diet should be made during the study without discussing first with the study team.


There is no cost to you for enrolling your cat in this study. Your cat will receive complimentary assessment and management of disease overseen by a board-certified specialist in feline CKD as well as standard of care laboratory monitoring regardless of study group. Cats may benefit from this therapy and can continue it after the study at the caretaker's expense.

Background and purpose

The Dog Aging Project is an innovative research initiative that brings together a community of dogs, their caretakers, veterinarians, researchers, and volunteers to carry out the most ambitious canine health study in the world. The Dog Aging Project team will follow tens of thousands of companion dogs for ten years or more in order to identify the biological, lifestyle, and environmental factors that maximize healthy longevity. We expect to gain insights that will increase our ability to prevent, diagnose, and treat age-related diseases, thereby helping our dogs, and by extension, ourselves, live longer, healthier lives. The goal of the Dog Aging Project is to understand how genes, lifestyle, and environment influence aging. We want to use that information to help companion dogs and people increase healthspan, the period of life spent free from disease.

Dogs truly are science’s best friends. Though they age more rapidly than humans, they get the same diseases of aging, have a rich genetic make-up, and share our environment. Like humans, they have a sophisticated healthcare system. By studying aging in dogs, we can more quickly expand our knowledge of the aging process not just in dogs but also in humans.


The Dog Aging Project includes expert scientists and research veterinarians from over 20 research institutions and veterinary teaching hospitals. Our core leadership is based at Tufts University and Texas A&M School of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences.


By enrolling in the Dog Aging Project, you are performing community science. Community science springs from the premise that anyone and everyone can think like a scientist. After all, at its most basic, scientific discovery is the result of a fundamental curiosity about the world and how it works. Scientists ask questions, make observations, design experiments, and collect data to answer our questions. You don’t need a PhD or a lab coat to make important contributions to the world’s body of knowledge. At the Dog Aging Project, we view the caretakers of enrolled dogs as key research partners. Our participants are the key to building an incredibly powerful dataset that will allow us to meet our scientific goals.


What happens in this study

If you’re interested in having your dog participate in the Dog Aging Project, please first visit the study website at https://dogagingproject.org/ to nominate your dog for enrollment. After nominating your dog, you will receive a link to create a personal research portal. You will be led through a comprehensive health and life experience survey about your dog's lifestyle, environment, health and daily activities.


In the health and life experience survey, you will have an opportunity to indicate whether or not you are willing to request and upload your dog's veterinary electronic medical records. This step is completely optional. If you chose to upload records, the Dog Aging Project team will review them and there may be opportunities to be offered participation in clinical trials associated with the Dog Aging Project.


​Some smaller studies within the Dog Aging Project look at enrolled companions' genetic backgrounds or annual biological sample lab results. At the same time, the clinical trial associated with the Dog Aging Project explores the potential of rapamycin to improve healthspan. Eligibility and invitation into the smaller studies or the clinical trial are determined by a set of scientific and statistical standards so that the Dog Aging Project can remain as unbiased as possible. Please remember that the main part of the Dog Aging Project is a longitudinal, observational study, meaning they will be monitoring the dogs from a distance without any intervention.


Please note, the only way to be offered enrollment in one of the associated clinical trials is to start at the Dog Aging Project website with nomination and completion of the health and life experience survey.


Pet owner responsibilities

If you're interesting in having your dog be a part of the Dog Aging Project, you will simply need to visit the Dog Aging Project website at https://dogagingproject.org/ and follow the steps to enroll your dog and complete the health and life experience survey.


Participation requirements

Dogs of any age, sex, breed, and health status, living within the United States are invited to participate in the Dog Aging Project


Benefits and risks of participating

This is an observational, data-collection study only, and is not designed or intended to diagnose or treat any disease or condition. There are no direct benefits to your dog for participation in this study. However, participation greatly helps us learn more about the aging process in dogs and can potentially help benefit future companions.


Compensation

Enrollment in this study is on a volunteer basis. There is no compensation for those who enroll their dogs in the Dog Aging Project. There is no cost to participate.

Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.

Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

Background and Purpose of the Trial

Epilepsy is reported to affect around 5% of the canine population, making it the most common neurologic condition in dogs. There are currently a very limited number of antiepileptic drugs (AEDS) available to treat epilepsy in dogs. The primary choice of AED is currently phenobarbital which, while typically effective, can come with side effects that can be hard for both the pet and the pet owner. Studies have shown that CBD can be effective in decreasing seizures when added to a primary AED and we are now exploring if CBD can be an effective primary therapy on its own. Dogs in this study will be randomly assigned to either phenobarbital or CBD at the beginning of the study. Over the course of the first 8 weeks, the dose may be titrated up; starting at week 8, the dose can no longer be adjusted, and no other medications can be added in without needing to withdraw the pet. At the end of the study, owners and the clinician will be unblinded to ensure the pet can continue the appropriate medication or make adjustments as needed.


Who Qualifies

  1. Dogs must be between the ages of 1 – 6 years when the first seizure occurs
  2. Dogs cannot currently be on any anti-seizure medications
  3. Dogs must have had at least 2 seizures in 6 weeks, with at least 24 hours separating the seizures
  4. Dogs must be otherwise healthy
  5. Owners must be willing to keep a detailed seizure log throughout the study

Study Design


Visit 1 | Day 0

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Verify eligibility criteria
  3. Blood draw for baseline blood levels
  4. Oral cotton swab for DNA analysis
  5. Start CBD or phenobarbital (owner will receive an oil and a pill, each to be dosed twice daily)
  6. Titrate dosing up if needed

Visit 2 | Day 14

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 3 | Day 56

  1. End of titration period
  2. Neurologic exam
  3. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 4 | Day 98

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels

Visit 5 | Day 140

  1. Neurologic exam
  2. Blood draw for a complete blood cell count, chemistry profile, and drug levels
  3. One month of study drug to owner, along with instructions for continued use or discontinuation as needed

Financial Incentives

All exams, along with the study medication, will be covered by the study. Additionally, at the end of the study, the owner will receive a one-month supply of the drug the pet was on in order to continue dosing or transition to a different medication if needed.

B cell lymphoma impacts >250,000 dogs every year. The current standard of care is CHOP chemotherapy, a multi-agent protocol that takes 3-4 months of trips to the vet and costs $7,000-12,000 while only extending the life of a pet 10-12 months.


This clinical trial is evaluating the safety and efficacy of Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in dogs with B cell lymphoma. CAR-T cells are a type of engineered T cell (an immune cell found in mammals) that have had a series of genes added to them that make them professional killers of cancer cells expressing certain shapes, called antigens. In this trial for B cell lymphoma, the antigen the CAR-T cells will target is called CD20. CAR-T cell therapy is FDA approved for multiple blood cancers in humans and is a revolution in how cancer is treated, bringing cures to patients who have no other treatment options.


This clinical trial seeks to better understand the effects of the CAR-T cells on lymph node tumors and internal disease, as well as how CAR-T cells influence the dog’s immune system to re-activate and fight cancer on its own. The trial will also test different pre-treatments, determined based on the additive measurements of four target lymph nodes (called the "sum of longest diameters").


This trial is sponsored by LEAH Labs, a biotechnology company building living therapies for pets with cancer. The trial is 100% funded from enrollment, provides a generous adverse event stipend, and offers a stipend for future care.

 Some cats are at risk of developing a condition called chylothorax. Chylothorax can occur because of a “leaky vessel” (known as the thoracic duct), which can cause accumulation of fluid (chyle) in the chest cavity. This excess of fluid within the chest cavity can impair the lungs during breathing and result in potentially life-threatening situations. Treatment of chylothorax in cats typically requires surgery to close the thoracic duct, preventing fluid from leaking into the chest cavity. Traditionally, surgical intervention of chylothorax requires opening the abdominal and chest cavities, causing a considerable amount of discomfort and even pain after surgery. Minimally invasive approaches have been developed, like thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation where closure is performed through small incisions with the use of a camera and specialized instruments. The addition of another technique, known as pericardiectomy (removal of the pericardium, which is a sac-like organ surrounding the heart) along with thoracic duct repair is often performed to reduce the chance of recurrence. Even with these techniques in combination, recurrence rates of up to 30-50% have been reported. Additionally, more recent studies suggest that pericardiectomy may not be necessary in all patients, but rather proper identification of the location of the thoracic duct before surgery by way of a CT scan and in surgery by way of contrast can improve outcomes for cats.


     Currently, there are no prospective studies for cats with idiopathic chylothorax using standardized preoperative diagnostics and surgical techniques for each patient. This includes the use of contrast material before and during surgery to better identify the thoracic duct and stop its flow at the proper location, which is highly dependent on each cat. The aim of this project is to assess the outcome of cats with idiopathic chylothorax undergoing thoracoscopic thoracic duct ligation who have a standardized diagnostic workup preoperatively and successful preoperative and intraoperative thoracic duct visualization.


Cats are invited to participate in this study if they are at least 6.6 lbs (3 kg) or greater, greater than 2 years of age, and have been diagnosed with idiopathic chylothorax. Prior to inclusion into this study cats will undergo physical examination and be diagnosed with chylothorax using pleural effusion fluid analysis (abnormal buildup of fluid in the pleural space, which is a thin cavity between the lungs and the chest wall). If not already completed within two weeks of their planned surgery date, cats will undergo a complete physical examination, and blood will be collected for complete blood count and serum biochemistry prior to admittance in this study. Additionally, cats will receive a complete work-up for chylothorax including an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound), heartworm testing, chest x-rays, and pleural effusion fluid analysis. If cats have undergone surgery previously for chylothorax or if they have an identified underlying cause of chylothorax (e.g. cancer, heart disease, lung lobe torsion, etc.), they will be excluded from participation in this study.


Cats will be placed under general anesthesia for their first procedure. A CT scan will be conducted first, where a contrast solution (iohexol) will be injected underneath the skin around the anus and/or into the metatarsal paw pads, to highlight the thoracic duct. Under the same anesthetic event, your cat will also have a small incision made into its neck and a catheter will be placed in the jugular vein to measure pressures at the level of the heart.

At a later date, cats will be placed under anesthesia again for surgery. Three very small (5-10mm) incisions will be made near the ribs for insertion of special surgical instruments (thoracoscopic camera and instruments) to allow the surgeon to see inside the chest cavity and close the thoracic duct branches. The thoracic duct will be visualized using a dye injected around the anus prior to surgery. If the thoracic duct is unable to be visualized with this minimally invasive technique, an incision will be made into the chest cavity between two of the ribs and the surgery will proceed as an “open” thoracic duct ligation. A chest tube will be placed to monitor post-operative fluid production in all patients, as is standard of care for chylothorax patients.


All enrolled cats will be hospitalized post-operatively in the intensive care unit for a minimum of 48 hours for monitoring. Cats will be sent home once they are voluntarily eating and drinking, and their pain is deemed appropriately controlled with oral medications. All cats must be re-evaluated at the UF Small Animal Hospital at 1-, 3-, and 6 months after surgery for physical exam and chest x-rays to confirm occlusion of the thoracic duct and resolution of chylothorax. A repeat CT scan under anesthesia will be performed at 3 months post-surgery, or sooner if clinical signs reoccur before then.
